entry.title: Sixty-three functions deferred for a checker gap that was not there
entry.summary: Since checker version 5 went live, production lanes had deferred sixty-three functions with one reason: the function reads data through an absolute address that has no relocation entry, and the checker option that serves such reads cannot work on this machine. The coordinator took that at face value for half a day, reported it as a growing cost, and started a checker lane to build a replacement for the option. That lane found the real cause before it was cut off: the functions have no such addresses. Checked independently, not one of the sixty-three does.
entry.content:
Since checker version 5 went live, production lanes had deferred sixty-three functions with one reason: the function reads data through an absolute address that has no relocation entry, and the checker option that serves such reads cannot work on this machine. The coordinator took that at face value for half a day, reported it as a growing cost, and started a checker lane to build a replacement for the option. That lane found the real cause before it was cut off: the functions have no such addresses. Checked independently, not one of the sixty-three does.

FactValueWhat it means
Functions deferred for this reason63, in about fifteen lanesMost are in the ped-task code, where functions reference many global tables.
Absolute in-image operands in those functions674Counted by disassembling each function and taking every four-byte operand whose value lies inside the program's image.
Of those, without a relocation entry4All four are bit masks that happen to fall in the image's address range. None is an address.
Functions that truly need the option0The stock checker applies every relocation entry when it loads the original; these functions run as they are.

How sixty-three lanes' worth of care went wrong the same way

The relocation table is stored in blocks. Each entry is a small offset within its block. The library the lanes use to read the file already adds the block's base and reports each entry's complete address. The lanes' audits added the block's base again, so every address they looked up was wrong, no entry ever matched, and every absolute operand looked unrelocated. The audit was written carefully, with counts and cross-checks, and it was wrong in one line. Status: Verified, by the checker lane's note and by an independent count.

The coordinator made it worse. The brief for version 5 introduced the deferral reason and told lanes to use it when a function reads through an unrelocated address, without giving them a correct way to tell. A rule that names an exit without a test for it invites exactly this: a plausible audit, a confident deferral, and no proof run, because the brief also says not to spend time proving a known gap again.

What was decided

  • A script now does the check correctly for any function and lists the operands that truly lack an entry. The production brief (version b11) forbids deferring for this reason on a lane's own audit and tells lanes to run the script first.
  • Four re-run lanes took the sixty-three functions back to verify them on the stock checker.
  • The replacement checker option the second checker lane built (contract-declared relocations, with passing proofs and an identical regression) is kept in its scratch folder but is not planned for installation: there is no longer a known function that needs it.
  • An earlier case is now suspect for the same reason: three functions deferred as reading writable data through unrelocated addresses. They are to be checked with the same script.
  • Rule for the coordinator: a deferral reason that a brief introduces must come with a machine check for it, and the first handful of deferrals under a new reason are verified independently before the reason is trusted.

To reproduce: for a deferred function, disassemble it from the mapped image, collect the four-byte operands whose value lies inside the image, and look each operand's position up in the set of relocation entry addresses as the library reports them, with nothing added.

entry.title: Naming the event vtable: one batch pins down twelve virtual slots
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions in the event system turned out to be overrides of twelve shared virtual slots plus their helpers, and the slot meanings are now evidence-backed and reusable: 148 named, 2 honestly left empty.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions in the event system turned out to be overrides of twelve shared virtual slots plus their helpers, and the slot meanings are now evidence-backed and reusable: 148 named, 2 honestly left empty.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and naming each function in project style, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified The batch is runs of overrides of the same virtual slots across the event class hierarchy, so each slot needed one identification that then named a whole run.

SlotMeaningEvidence
1event type idthe handler dispatch routine switches on its return value
2event priority idprecedence comparisons order on it
4 and 21clonepool allocate then copy-construct, forty identical bodies
5per-ped updaterecomputes loudness, ticks timers, issues one-shot tasks
8whether the event affects a pedbool predicates over ped tasks, groups, intel and loudness; subclasses reuse one implementation
10 and 13subject ped and subject entityresolve the subject, including vehicle to driver; slot 10 additionally gates on ped activity
14whether this event supersedes anothersame-subject checks used by a list dedup helper
15audible rangeconstant per class, consumed as the range in a loudness falloff
17whether the event is still validvalidity window in the base, ped-liveness gates in overrides
20whether this event takes priority over anothercompares type ids and priorities of two events

Verified The surrounding helpers form an inform pipeline: a loudness helper combining event range with distance falloff, a type-compatibility table with clear, register and query sides, and two inform tables (friends and group) with reset, schedule, per-frame update and per-slot fire functions, plus routines that inform nearby friends, a ped group and vehicle occupants.

Inferred Two large decision-maker evaluation stages were understood structurally but left unnamed because their exact contract stayed unclear; they need their shared evaluator identified first.

What was decided or recommended

Later naming lanes should reuse this slot table for event classes outside the batch instead of re-deriving each slot, and check the inform-table vocabulary against the neighbouring lane that named the find-or-add allocators. Clone-pattern bodies (pool allocate, null check, own constructor) can be named on sight.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the mapped image, group by vtable slot and signature, then confirm each slot by its consumers: who calls it, what it calls, and which sibling slots it reads. The decisive checks were the handler dispatch switch for the type slot, the precedence comparisons for the priority slot, and the init and per-frame call sites for the inform tables.

What was confusing or went wrong

A blind whole-image scan for virtual-slot call sites was too noisy to use, because every class has its own same-numbered slots; targeted reads near event-system code worked instead. Two inventory sizes overlap the following entry, so disassembly had to be cut at control-flow ends rather than at the listed size. The polarity of the validity slot and the exact contract of the decision stages could not be settled from static reading alone and are flagged for the next lane.

entry.title: Eight leaderboard routines verified, and a relocation-check trap
entry.summary: A batch of eight near-identical leaderboard polling routines is fully verified, after a wrong reading of the relocation table nearly had all eight deferred as unverifiable.
entry.content:
A batch of eight near-identical leaderboard polling routines is fully verified, after a wrong reading of the relocation table nearly had all eight deferred as unverifiable.

What was asked

Rewrite eight medium-sized routines from one leaderboard family in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original, with at least a thousand trials and a deliberately wrong version per routine.

What was found

Verified All eight routines verified with twelve hundred trials each, zero failures, and both wrong versions caught for every routine.

Verified The eight routines differ only in two constants, so one generator produced every rewrite and contract, asserting each member's shape first.

Verified A relocation-table check done through a parsing library reported the routines' switch tables as unrelocated, which would have made them unverifiable. Reading the raw table bytes showed the entries were present all along: the library's entry address is already absolute, and adding the block address double-counts it. A short probe confirmed the switch runs normally.

What was decided or recommended

Confirm any claim that an address lacks a relocation entry against the raw table bytes, and probe before deferring. The lane's driver copy also dumps the full call logs on the first failure, which is offered for folding back into the shared driver.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane generator to rebuild the eight rewrites and contracts, then run each contract through the stock checker driver. The wrong versions fail and the correct ones pass.

What was confusing or went wrong

The false unrelocated reading cost the most time: it pointed at deferral until the probe contradicted it. Two smaller rewrite bugs (a stale cursor value passed to one helper, a decrement leaking into the return value) and one contract bug (even-length answer cycles that starved half the helpers) were each caught by the checker and fixed.

entry.title: Eight leaderboard routines verified, and a relocation-check trap
entry.summary: A batch of eight near-identical leaderboard routines (one template routine instantiated per event) verified first-try on a shared contract once three rewrite bugs were fixed, but the lane nearly deferred the whole batch over a script bug that made healthy relocation entries invisible.
entry.content:
A batch of eight near-identical leaderboard routines (one template routine instantiated per event) verified first-try on a shared contract once three rewrite bugs were fixed, but the lane nearly deferred the whole batch over a script bug that made healthy relocation entries invisible.

What was asked

Rewrite eight medium-sized game functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the checker, generating all eight from one analysis since they sit side by side and share one shape.

What was found

Verified All eight routines are the same 113-instruction body differing only in one numeric id constant plus position-dependent branch targets, confirmed by hash over normalized disassembly and by per-member shape assertions in the generator.

Verified Each routine runs nineteen entries through two object calls and six helper calls: a selector answer picks one special entry per run, a filter skips entries, a five-way switch sets a step of eight or zero, the special entry may copy an eight-byte row, and other entries advance an unsigned cursor against a limit and write one bit into a mask. Two helper calls land in the encrypted first megabyte of the code section but are intercepted at the call site, so they never execute.

Verified The checker's relocation handling is fine for this family: every switch table and its address operand carries a relocation entry, so the relocated worker reads them correctly. An early script of mine added the relocation block base to an entry offset field that already contained the full address, which matched nothing and briefly made the tables look unrelocated. A sibling lane's script repeats the same double-add and has logged the same wrong conclusion; it should re-check before deferring on that ground.

Verified Three genuine rewrite bugs were caught by mismatches during probing, all fixed: an out-parameter script used the word index where the byte offset belonged, leaving a table pointer null; a commit helper receives the pre-advance cursor slot value rather than the advanced register; and the row-size gate is a signed comparison, so negative sizes copy.

What was decided or recommended

  • Record all eight as verified: 1200 passing trials each with full branch coverage and a caught wrong version per function.
  • Reuse the family-generator pattern (assert every member's call sites and id constant, then emit) for the sibling leaderboard batches.
  • When a relocation lookup finds nothing, distrust the lookup first: confirm the offset arithmetic against one known entry before concluding entries are missing.
  • The proof leaves three narrowings on record: incoming stack slots reused as scratch are not compared (their values are observed through call arguments and branches), the return is compared low-byte-only, and one frame-pointer call argument is uncompared by design.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the eight batch members and hash the normalized instruction text to confirm one shape; resolve every stack operand through a control-flow walk that models callee cleanup; generate one rewrite, one wrong version and one contract per member with a script that asserts each member's call sites and id constant; build one rewrite crate into the lane's own build folder; run the stock checker driver once per contract with at least a thousand trials plus the wrong-version run, and confirm every wrong version fails on the expected output.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The relocation false alarm cost about fifteen minutes and would have cost the batch: the double-added addresses silently matched nothing, which looks exactly like missing entries. The tell was a neighbouring lane hitting the identical wall at the same time, and the fix was reading one raw relocation block by hand.

Verified Two timestamps in the lane log were written from memory and were wrong by over half an hour; machine-written timestamps were used after the second one was caught.

Probe Result Cause
First Vacuous, both sides faulted on a third of trials Out-parameter offset pointed past the one-word script
Second Seven failures in sixty trials Stale cursor slot value passed to the commit helper
Third One failure in sixty trials Signed size gate misread as unsigned
Full runs Eight times 1200 of 1200, every wrong version caught Not applicable

entry.title: Naming batch 100: garages, shocking events, population, and three wrong native names
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions split into seven subsystems instead of one, and the batch yielded three corrections to the shared symbol table that matter for every lane working nearby.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions split into seven subsystems instead of one, and the batch yielded three corrections to the shared symbol table that matter for every lane working nearby.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name at high, medium, or low confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working from strings, callers, callees, classes, and read/write behaviour. No rewriting, no checker.

What was found

Verified The batch holds seven groups: a forty-record garage system with init, per-frame update, and save/load callbacks; a shocking-event task system driven by a thirty-one row info table; an ambient population system with spawning, scenario assignment, and streaming release; a small ped-roads group; spatial query helpers; a fragment and physics query cluster; and five event class constructors and destructors.

Verified The save system registers each block with its save callback pushed first and its load callback second, confirmed across four independent blocks. That ordering identifies the garage save and load functions.

Verified Comparing the event-info parser against the shipped data file columns identifies the min and max watch-time lookups and the weighted response picker.

Verified Three merged-symbol native attributions are wrong: one is the standard C random number generator, one returns the player vehicle or null, and one points at a ten-byte setter stub while the real native sits elsewhere. Two more merged names sit sixteen bytes before the true function starts.

Inferred Five small helpers in the encrypted first megabyte of code cannot be verified from the file at all; functions that depend on them were named by mechanics only.

What was decided or recommended

Twenty-one names at high confidence, one hundred fifteen at medium, fourteen left empty at low. For the next naming lane: scan for every reader and writer of a global before naming tiny setters, distrust a native name until the observed behaviour matches it, and read the shipped data file whenever a loader appears in the batch.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, never raw offsets. Build one evidence row per function with strings, imports, named callers and callees, and data references. Resolve each caller to its containing function through the merged symbols. Disassemble the heads of every load-bearing callee, and check push order at every call site of a registration helper before assigning callback roles.

What was confusing or went wrong

The inventory labelled nearly the whole batch as one subsystem, which was wrong for five of the seven groups. Two size-zero entries looked truncated until their tails past the first return were decoded. One truncated call list silently included the next function, and is only safe when every address is checked against the function end.

entry.title: Naming batch 99: what actually identifies a function
entry.summary: One hundred forty-four of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and nearly all of them were identified by their callers and callees rather than their own instructions.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-four of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and nearly all of them were identified by their callers and callees rather than their own instructions.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names with confidence levels for a batch of one hundred fifty unnamed, consecutive game functions spanning rendering, streaming, interiors, physics, ped tasks and car recordings.

What was found

Verified Attributing each unknown caller and callee to its containing function through the function inventory, then resolving lane and verified names for those containers, identified most of the batch. Callers included the game initialiser, the load-scene native, all five physical-attach natives, the apply-force natives and the set-frozen path.

Verified Small functions repay full reads: about ninety short functions were decoded completely, which settled direction questions such as get versus set and exposed three inventory size errors (one five-byte thunk listed as thousands of bytes, two real functions listed as size zero).

Verified Shape-matching against known relatives anchors virtual slots: the ped health setter calls the base health slot, and matching slot shapes confirmed the health, constructor and destructor names.

Verified Two widely-referenced shared stubs in the encrypted region are heap allocate and free, called from destructors, teardown and pool allocators; the merged symbol file labels one of them as a script native, which misdescribes every function that frees memory.

What was decided or recommended

Future naming lanes should attribute callers before reading bodies, fully decode short functions rather than sampling them, check inventory sizes against padding before trusting them, and distrust symbol names attached to encrypted-region stubs.

How to reproduce it

The lane scratch folder holds the evidence gatherer, the attribution script, the disassembly dumps and the per-function evidence table; rerunning the scripts against the executable and the inventory reproduces every claim.

What was confusing or went wrong

An operand-type constant bug silently captured zero calls on the first run and was caught by inspection. A home-made vtable matcher produced false slot attributions and was discarded in favour of the inventory tags. Six functions were left unnamed where the behaviour was readable but the purpose stayed unknown.

entry.title: Naming a batch of pickup, entity and object functions
entry.summary: 148 of 150 consecutive functions got names, most from direct reads plus three reusable signals: vtable slot sharing across classes, verified-rewrite docs for same-slot overrides, and RTTI class names.
entry.content:
148 of 150 consecutive functions got names, most from direct reads plus three reusable signals: vtable slot sharing across classes, verified-rewrite docs for same-slot overrides, and RTTI class names.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name with confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, then naming each one.

What was found

Verified The batch holds five clusters: a pickup pool with row create, delete, update and radius search; dynamic-entity lifetime, grid registration, bounds and drawing code; object physics, doors, damage, weapons and teleport; save and load dispatchers with pool helpers; and control-map loading, saving and menu rendering.

Verified Same vtable slot in one inheritance branch is the same method, so a verified doc comment for one class override names the slot for every class. This settled the bound getters, the bound-object creator, the list relink and the gated refresh.

Verified The class behind a vtable can be read from the type descriptor stored just before it. This gave exact names for two draw-command constructors that had no other signal.

Inferred Two grid functions form an add and remove pair for the sector grid. This disagrees with earlier names for the base-class versions of those slots, which describe flag and matrix work instead. Both readings are recorded and the conflict is flagged for joint review.

What was decided or recommended

Give each function the name of the behaviour actually read, even when a sibling class carries a different earlier name, and record the disagreement plainly. The next naming lane should reuse the slot map, the verified docs and the RTTI trick before reading instructions.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per batch with a script: disassemble each function from the mapped image, collect direct calls, import calls, string references, callers from a full code scan, and vtable references from a data scan. Resolve the introducing class of each virtual from the structure dumps, look up same-slot names in other classes, read the small and unclear functions fully, then name from the table.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first megabyte of code is encrypted on disk, so several dozen callees disassemble as garbage. Two functions that only forward into that region were left unnamed. Some existing symbol labels are known-wrong placeholders and had to be worked around rather than trusted.

entry.title: Encrypted-target calls can be verified after all
entry.summary: Verified Direct calls whose target lies in the encrypted first megabyte of code verify like any other intercepted call: the checker patches the call site, the stub answers, and the encrypted bytes never execute. One function with four such calls passed all 1100 trials.
entry.content:
Verified Direct calls whose target lies in the encrypted first megabyte of code verify like any other intercepted call: the checker patches the call site, the stub answers, and the encrypted bytes never execute. One function with four such calls passed all 1100 trials.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring task-system functions and prove each identical to the original. Two were flagged as likely needing encrypted code.

What was found

Verified Four of five verified (1000-1100 trials each, every wrong version caught). The fifth is staged: its entry paths pass and the loop body has a complete plan.

Verified The genuine encrypted-code cases are narrow: the function itself lives in the encrypted region, an indirect call whose pointer cannot be built, or a code read. A plain direct call to an encrypted address is none of these, though its signature must be read from the caller side (what is pushed, who cleans up, how the result is used).

Verified One function holds a direct call to an odd address inside writable data, gated by a flag and with its result ignored. What it means is unknown.

What was decided or recommended

Patch direct calls into the encrypted region instead of deferring them, and defer only what the original must actually execute there. The lane brief should say this.

How to reproduce it

Declare the encrypted-target call as a normal patched callee with caller-derived signature (argument count from pushes, cleanup from stack balance, return channel from use) and run the stock checker; the original completes trials instead of faulting.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two false alarms about missing relocations were my own disp-offset slips (three-byte opcodes take their address at a different offset than four-byte ones). A countdown loop ran eleven times, not ten, because it exits on sign. Pin cycles with equal periods silently hid whole branch classes until an exact path enumerator exposed them.

entry.title: Naming a batch of game functions: weapons, pads, cameras
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be five separate groups: gamepad rumble and state handling, weapon data parsing, vehicle and zone helpers, viewport and render-target code, and game camera logic. Just over two thirds could be named with confidence.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be five separate groups: gamepad rumble and state handling, weapon data parsing, vehicle and zone helpers, viewport and render-target code, and game camera logic. Just over two thirds could be named with confidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each function in the batch, with a confidence level and one sentence of evidence, working from strings, called functions, neighbouring names, and class layout information.

What was found

Verified Seven near-identical string-matching routines each scan a table of recognised words. Reading those tables gave exact domains: damage types, explosion types, fire types, fuse types, weapon flag words, stat types, and weapon slots.

Verified The larger parsing routines reference plain field names for accuracy, rates, ranges, melee groups, and explosion thresholds, and open the weapon data file. The batch holds the whole weapon information loader.

Verified Two inventory subsystem labels were wrong: the supposed streaming code at the start of the batch is gamepad input handling, and the supposed network code at the end is game camera logic plus pickup handling.

Inferred The camera code includes the game camera's deleting destructor, its idle reset and restart steps, a per-frame update, and many small create, find, and flag helpers. The viewport code includes refresh and release steps plus child-list maintenance.

What was decided or recommended

One hundred and five functions were named and forty-five left unnamed where the evidence only showed a bare getter, a leaf arithmetic routine, or calls into still-unknown helpers. The next naming lane covering nearby code should distrust subsystem labels and re-derive the group from strings first.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the mapped image, collect direct call targets, referenced strings, and nearby merged names into one table, then read the short functions and decode any string tables the matchers scan. Vtable membership is confirmed by finding data words that point at the function.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first read path mixed up file offsets with mapped-image offsets, shifting every disassembly by a constant. The shifted bytes still decoded into plausible-looking code with self-consistent call targets, which hid the mistake until vtable targets failed to decode as real methods. The fix was to read through the library's address-to-data call, and a good tripwire is that genuine vtable targets always decode as clean method prologues.

entry.title: Checker extension: doubles in vector registers across calls
entry.summary: The checker can now observe double-precision values passed in vector registers to helper calls, the gap that was deferring the most functions. Three deferred functions pass at full trial counts with their wrong versions caught on the new build.
entry.content:
The checker can now observe double-precision values passed in vector registers to helper calls, the gap that was deferring the most functions. Three deferred functions pass at full trial counts with their wrong versions caught on the new build.

What was asked

Production lanes had deferred several functions whose helpers take doubles in vector registers and answer doubles the same way. The checker moved only four bytes per vector register from the rewrite side and exposed only the low word of a double answer, so wrong versions that changed doubles passed every trial. The task was to add opt-in contract options for eight-byte vector call arguments and full double answers, prove them the way the existing self-test proofs do, show every existing verdict unchanged, and re-run the deferred functions.

What was found

Verified The call log already records and compares all sixteen bytes of each selected vector register; the four-byte limits were the rewrite-side transport (one single-precision move), the answer channel (low word only reached the rewrite), and nothing else. Entry values and the tested function's own vector return already travelled at full width.

Verified Probing the real calls showed the upper halves of the argument registers hold conversion residue the helper never reads: a constant pair of negative float zeros in two cases, zeros elsewhere. A rewrite-side move zeroes the upper half unconditionally, so comparing all sixteen bytes could never match; the new comparison covers the low eight bytes each helper actually reads and says so in the verdict.

Verified Four self-test proofs behave as designed: the correct rewrite passes a thousand trials, a wrong double argument and an ignored double answer are each caught, a contract without the new options lets the wrong version pass as a control, and an entry-width proof confirms all sixteen bytes reach both sides.

Verified Regression: every contract with a recorded verdict or mutant verdict gives the identical result on the new build, and the standalone validator reports identical results on every tracked contract.

  • Three deferred functions now pass at full trial counts with their wrong versions caught, recorded as ready for a stock re-run (not verified: the build is not stock until reviewed and installed).
  • Five more deferred functions stay blocked: four kept no rewrite or only a staged plan, and one large function needs its staged regions unpinned across five helper sites, which is production work beyond this lane.

Inferred One kept rewrite reads its helper's answer through the floating-point stack, which the stand-in never touches, yet passes because every scripted answer in its contract narrows to positive zero. Its pass may depend on how this machine's emulation handles an empty-stack read, so the adapted rewrite for the re-run avoids that path.

What was decided or recommended

The extension is proposed for review and installation: an eight-byte rewrite-side move per register, a double answer delivered to both sides, low-eight-byte comparison per register, scripted doubles, and per-trial double entry values, all off unless a contract asks and all recorded in the verdict. Still missing and recommended next: a way for a rewrite to return a vector value, which keeps vector-returning originals unverifiable, and production lanes for the five functions that stay blocked.

How to reproduce it

Build the worker and the proofs library from the lane's tree with the lane target directory, run the driver's self-test, then run the four new self-test proof contracts: the correct rewrites pass a thousand trials each, the wrong versions fail, and the documented negative passes. Re-run every existing contract except the one needing the read-only shadow option and compare each verdict and mutant verdict with the record. Rebuild each adapted re-run crate into the path its adapted contract names and run it with the new driver.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first adapted re-run faulted on every trial that reached the helper call. Tracing the fault showed a register holding zero where the object pointer belonged, which first suggested the new stub code clobbered a preserved register. It had not: the adaptation had reused the parameter's name for a double's low word, shadowing it, so a later call received the word instead of the pointer. Renaming the locals fixed it. Separately, two log timestamps were written from memory and corrected from the clock, and one rebuild was briefly locked by a transient file handle.

entry.title: Naming batch 95: shader globals, deferred lighting, and wheels misfiled as audio
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be lights, a ped bone-damage shader effect, shader-global setters, wheel and tyre simulation, deferred lighting setup, an audio grid, and UI plus render phases, and the batch produced reusable parameter maps along with several earlier names that now look wrong.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be lights, a ped bone-damage shader effect, shader-global setters, wheel and tyre simulation, deferred lighting setup, an audio grid, and UI plus render phases, and the batch produced reusable parameter maps along with several earlier names that now look wrong.

What was asked

Name each function in the batch from evidence, strongest first: referenced strings, called imports, known callers and callees, class and virtual-table analysis, then behaviour.

What was found

Verified The shader-global setters form one family: an init routine binds handles for the scalar, screen-size, fog, depth-effect, day-night and stencil globals, and each setter matches its handle and cache entry exactly. The same family contains an already-verified rewrite whose stream name does not fit what it sets.

Verified The deferred-lighting setup resolves about forty named handles for lights, g-buffer textures, shadow params and reflection, and a separate refresh routine creates the g-buffer, stencil and back-z targets from name strings. Two small getters return the g-buffer-3 and stencil handles.

Verified The wheel code owns two objects: a small wheel-data record with a twelve-slot pool and registry, and a larger wheel-state object holding a burst level and flag words. All five large math kernels in the group touch those same state words.

Inferred Those wheel kernels are called from functions named as audio mixers, one of them verified. Either the mixers are vehicle-update code under the wrong name or the kernels serve both systems; the shared object size and field offsets lean toward misnamed callers.

Inferred Two merged native names collide with shared stubs: one address every deleting destructor calls to free memory, and one the lights and wheel kernels call as a math helper. Native-mapped names on shared stubs should not be trusted.

What was decided or recommended

  • Name the 146 functions the evidence supports and leave 4 empty rather than guess.
  • Flag the suspect earlier names for re-examination instead of renaming them from this lane.
  • Recommend the next naming lane decode the render-state number enum, which would sharpen about ten state-block names.

How to reproduce it

Read code only through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address, and decode one known function end to end first. Gather strings, imports, callees and callers per function into one table, resolve callers through the function-inventory ranges rather than nearest names, confirm every class claim against its virtual table, then read the short functions fully and the large ones by call context.

What was confusing or went wrong

Nearest-name caller attribution was wrong for about one call in seven, with offsets reaching far into huge neighbouring functions; every caller claim had to be re-resolved through inventory ranges. The encrypted low-memory helpers forced all callee-side reasoning onto strings and data flow. Two render-phase virtual slots both carry the name render from different lanes, and only one of them can be right.

entry.title: Naming a render-list batch: bleed, merged entries and the encrypted megabyte
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions in the render-list and timecycle region were named from strings, known callees and verified-rewrite docs, with eight left empty where the evidence ran out.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions in the render-list and timecycle region were named from strings, known callees and verified-rewrite docs, with eight left empty where the evidence ran out.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name at high, medium or low confidence for each function in the batch, working out what the group is about first and leaving the name empty when the function cannot be identified.

What was found

Verified The batch is one coherent region: render phases and their callbacks, two occupancy grids, MLO and stream render lists, a key-value sort family, timecycle and visual-settings code, and drawable streaming. The inventory subsystem labels on the range are partly wrong.

Verified Disassembling past a listed size attributes the next function calls and strings to short functions. Two names here would have been wrong from that alone; every name was re-checked against the exact-size body.

Verified Three listed entries contain a second unlisted function in their byte range, one listed entry is the tail fragment of its predecessor, and two sizes end a few bytes early. The fragment was left unnamed.

Verified Calls below the half-megabyte mark decode as garbage because that region is encrypted on disk; those callees were identified only from verified-rewrite docs or usage shape, never from disassembly.

Inferred Several bare constant getters return render-list cursor bases, but only the one tied to a developer overflow message could be identified; the rest were left empty rather than guessed.

What was decided or recommended

Named 142 of 150 functions: 38 high, 104 medium, 8 low and empty. Callback invokes follow the established full-signature style. The fragment and merged entries were reported to the coordinator for inventory fixes. New subsystem labels timecycle and core were used where the existing labels did not fit.

How to reproduce it

Read code only through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address. Build one evidence table for the whole batch first (calls resolved against merged names, lane names and the verified index; immediates against a string table; indirect calls against imports), read the short bodies exactly, then name from the strongest evidence: verified docs first, strings second, class identity third.

What was confusing or went wrong

The evidence script initially disassembled past each listed size, which silently attached neighbour calls and strings to short functions and survived two reviews before a full-body read exposed it. Timestamps written from memory were wrong twice and had to be corrected from the machine clock.

entry.title: Naming batch: streaming emitters, player variation, and a mislabelled lights cluster
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions split into five groups: a streaming request pipeline, player variation and ped components, prop draw setup with kd-tree utilities, and a lights and draw-command cluster that the inventory labels network and input-ui. All but four were named.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions split into five groups: a streaming request pipeline, player variation and ped components, prop draw setup with kd-tree utilities, and a lights and draw-command cluster that the inventory labels network and input-ui. All but four were named.

What was asked

Name each function in the batch from static evidence only: referenced strings, called imports, known callers and callees, virtual tables, and read/write behaviour. No rewriting and no checker.

What was found

Verified The streaming group is one pipeline: eight request emitters funnel into a single shared hub, which dispatches to a minimal builder and a frag dispatcher, with builders stamping a small state tag and five thunks adapting three embedded intrusive lists to shared push and pop helpers. One function is the per-tick streaming update, recognised by its stability gate, request aging, release, rebalance and culling steps.

Verified The player variation group holds the cores behind the set-component-variation script natives, a call-free hash slot lookup used from eight directions, player diff table building, and a full and partial record init pair.

Verified Seven functions sit in RTTI virtual tables as the invoke slot of callback functors and draw-command classes, confirmed by reading the raw table bytes, and two more construct such objects. Three allocator stubs each bake a different worker address into the command they allocate, which explains why those workers have no direct callers.

Verified Two inventory entries listed with size zero are real functions with named callers, one padded entry starts in the tail of its predecessor, and one stub size overruns into its siblings. The subsystem labels for the lights cluster are wrong.

What was decided or recommended

  • Confirm every RTTI table hit by reading the raw table bytes before naming from it; it is cheap and decisive.
  • Cite a string only when the code uses it as one; a comparison against a single config byte next to a string blob is not string evidence.
  • Distrust caller hits that fall inside no known function; they are usually false positives from byte scanning.
  • Leave functions rooted in the encrypted code region unnamed when nothing else identifies them.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch first (calls resolved against the merged name databases, imports, strings, data references, memory accesses), then scan the code section for direct callers attributed to containing inventory functions, then check RTTI table slots and raw table bytes, then read only the short and unclear functions directly.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified A prior retry kit describes two kd-tree scans as min-scans; a flag-level read shows the select keeps the strictly greater element, so they are max-scans. A zlib error string match turned out to be a config byte sitting next to the string, not a use of it. One shared stub carries a script-native name in the symbol table but is called per entry by unrelated table-clearing code, so that name is suspect.

entry.title: Six task-system functions verified, and a stub write that drops its first word
entry.summary: A production batch of six neighbouring task-system functions was rewritten in Rust and all six passed 1,200 checker trials each with their own wrong versions caught. The batch also surfaced a checker quirk worth knowing: a scripted callee output through a register silently drops its first word.
entry.content:
A production batch of six neighbouring task-system functions was rewritten in Rust and all six passed 1,200 checker trials each with their own wrong versions caught. The batch also surfaced a checker quirk worth knowing: a scripted callee output through a register silently drops its first word.

What was asked

Rewrite six original game functions from the pedestrian task subsystem in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version 5 checker, with contracts covering calls, globals, floats and faults.

What was found

Verified All six functions passed with zero failures across 7,200 trials, including fault-parity trials where both sides crash identically on null records. The functions form one pipeline: a parameter-block copy, a template builder, a flag-driven dispatcher, two kind-word gates, and a 24-arm record lookup.

Verified A scripted callee output of four words through a register lands words two to four correctly but leaves word zero as ambient stack garbage. Two words of evidence: with a zero script the snapshot showed garbage in word zero and zeros after; with a distinctive script it showed the same garbage followed by the scripted words. The emitter source reads correctly, so the cause is still open. It fails closed: contracts relying on word zero get a mismatch, never a false pass.

Verified Cycled contract values with related lengths can lock together so a branch never fires: one pin layout made ten lookup arms unreachable because the needed handle kind always coincided with a null-handle trial. Coprime cycle lengths plus a 30-line simulator that replays all trial phases fixed it and now proves every arm fires at least 22 times.

What was decided or recommended

  • Route around the dropped first word by scripting and snapshotting from the second word on (offset write plus offset snapshot), and disclose the uncompared word.
  • Run a phase simulation over pin, global and script cycles for any contract with a multi-arm switch; the checker's branch count is too coarse to confirm arm coverage.
  • When pushed words and stack cleanup disagree at a call, trust the balanced return to derive the callee's pop count.

How to reproduce it

Check any production contract that scripts a register output and snapshots it: set the script to distinctive words and compare the snapshot's first word against them. For the phase check, replay the contract's cycle lengths over the trial count and assert each needed value combination occurs.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two hex stack offsets were mis-added as decimal, producing an elaborate but false theory that a function leaked its entry registers into a call argument. Distinctive-value probes disproved it in minutes: the slot held a pinned callee answer, and the rewrite simplified to one line. Twice now, reading offsets in a hurry has cost more than the probe that checks them.

entry.title: Naming the particle-effects region: signals that worked
entry.summary: Naming 150 consecutive functions across the particle-effects and streaming-slot code named 141 of them, and the same small set of code shapes identified nearly every one.
entry.content:
Naming 150 consecutive functions across the particle-effects and streaming-slot code named 141 of them, and the same small set of code shapes identified nearly every one.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 unnamed functions with a confidence each, working out what the group is about first and reading code through the executable's mapped image rather than raw file offsets.

What was found

Verified The span holds the game's particle-effect machinery in rough order: fade channels, streaming entry handling, the particle manager and its frame update, a queue of effect requests, one emitter function per water effect, surface and impact dispatch, the weapon-effect table loader, weapon emitters, and spatial lookup kernels.

Verified The most reliable naming signals, strongest first:

  • Effect-name strings plus a shared replay-gate prelude identify emitters almost mechanically; each water effect has one function.
  • Named callees from already verified neighbours (slot, fade, audio and particle helpers) name the glue code between them.
  • This-adjusting jumps resolve to five list primitives (push front and back, pop front, remove, clear), which names every queue thunk.
  • A thread-storage row pattern (slot flags, row index, fixed stride) marks four identical float accessors and two functions that inline it.
  • A 255.0 scale factor shows a converter makes an alpha byte, confirmed by its caller using the result as alpha.

Verified Three inventory entries are not functions: two are code tails plus padding with the real entry point bytes later, and one label sits inside another function's loop while covering a stub and an emitter.

Inferred Nine functions were left unnamed: the three non-functions, two that call only into the encrypted first megabyte of code, one caller of an undetermined routine, and three large math kernels whose roles never became clear.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the vocabulary the verified neighbours already established, with an emit suffix for one-effect emitter functions and a thunk suffix for jumps to known targets. The next naming lane in nearby code should learn the replay-gate prelude and the list primitives first, since they recur constantly, and should treat any callee in the encrypted region as opaque rather than guessing.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per function (referenced strings, imports called, named callees and callers, data references) from the memory-mapped image, verify the mapping on one known function, then read the short and unclear functions fully and name from the table. Heads plus tails of large functions were enough; only a handful needed a middle read.

What was confusing or went wrong

A promising compression-library string hit turned out to be a byte comparison against a global flag that merely sits next to unrelated text, not a string reference at all. A byte-scan caller search also reported callers that vanish under real disassembly, because the matched byte sits inside another instruction. Both now get a second check before being trusted.

entry.title: A one-line address bug that fakes an unverifiable verdict
entry.summary: A production lane nearly deferred its whole batch as unverifiable because a triage script misread the executable's relocation table; the corrected check showed every absolute operand was relocatable after all, and five of the six functions then verified on the first or second attempt.
entry.content:
A production lane nearly deferred its whole batch as unverifiable because a triage script misread the executable's relocation table; the corrected check showed every absolute operand was relocatable after all, and five of the six functions then verified on the first or second attempt.

What was asked

Rewrite six neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each one bit-identical to the original with the project checker, deferring with a reason code only those the checker cannot verify.

What was found

Verified The lane's first triage script reported that almost every absolute memory operand in the batch lacked a relocation entry, which would have made the functions untestable on this machine. The script was wrong: it added each relocation block's base address to an entry value that already included it, so it looked the addresses up in a garbage set and found nothing. The single step that exposed it was a pinned experiment: with game data forced to a known value, the original still matched the rewrite exactly, which is only possible if the original reads relocated game data.

Verified After the fix, zero of seventy-five absolute operands in the batch lacked entries, and five functions passed twelve hundred trials each with deliberately wrong versions caught every time. The sixth function keeps a passing entry-stage proof while its long owner path waits for a full lane with a retry kit.

Inferred Other lanes defer functions for the same stated reason, citing some of the same data words; any deferral whose only evidence is a script using the same address recipe should be re-checked, because the recipe fails silently and always in the same direction.

What was decided or recommended

The lane verified five functions instead of deferring six, and recommends that every relocation check be confirmed by behaviour (a short pinned run) rather than trusted from a script alone, and that past unverifiable verdicts resting only on such a script be audited.

How to reproduce it

Parse the relocation directory with the standard library recipe, then test one known operand two ways: membership of its address in the parsed set, and a short checker run with the pointed-to game word forced to two different values. If the run tracks the forced values, the operand is relocated whatever the script says.

What was confusing or went wrong

The wrong triage looked authoritative: exact counts, consistent failures, and matching precedent from sibling lanes. Two further hours of analysis nearly followed it. What broke the spell was not more analysis but one small experiment whose result the wrong theory could not produce. The lane also learned, twice, that snapshot and store positions must be derived from an exact stack-depth trace rather than adjusted by hand: both mid-lane failures were off-by-one-slot mapping slips, found by narrowing snapshots to single words.

entry.title: Naming a batch of interior and streaming functions
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be two clean clusters, interior rooms and portals followed by IPL and streaming-device code, and caller context proved to be the strongest naming signal after verified callee names.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be two clean clusters, interior rooms and portals followed by IPL and streaming-device code, and caller context proved to be the strongest naming signal after verified callee names.

What was asked

Name each of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed game functions in address order, with a confidence per name and evidence for later tooling. No rewriting, only names.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into two clusters: about sixty functions around interior instances (rooms, portals, room states, bounds, placement, including one class's virtual slots twenty to twenty-seven) and about ninety around the IPL store and the streaming device (slot requests, a quadtree index, stream entries, loader callbacks).

Verified One hundred and thirty-one functions were named: thirteen high confidence, one hundred and eighteen medium, nineteen left empty at low. Useful fixed points included pool-creation strings, the wanted-bit loop issuing IPL request and remove calls, a quadtree family of six, and cost-subtract twins differing only in which totals they touch.

Verified A whole-text call scan found callers for one hundred and seventeen of the one hundred and fifty functions, and reading those call sites upgraded six names from low to medium, including two flag bits whose tester callers (portal tracker, vertex lookup, teardown, config load) revealed their purpose.

Inferred The per-model room definitions live behind a global table indexed by model number, with room arrays in fixed strides and per-instance state arrays; the stream entries follow the twenty-four byte layout the verified rewrites document.

What was decided or recommended

  • Single-bit flag tests stay unnamed unless their callers reveal the bit's meaning; eleven bits were tested and only three earned names.
  • Jump aliases that overlap the next function's padding get the target's name plus a thunk suffix at the same confidence, so the alias is findable without inventing a distinction.
  • Functions whose core callees sit in the encrypted region stay unnamed; the archive-handling tail of this batch is in that state.
  • Caller attribution must check the current batch's own ranges first, because nearest-named-below matching points at the wrong function whenever the true caller is itself unnamed.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch first (callee names from the merged symbol sources, referenced strings, constants, memory access shapes), validate the address mapping against known jump targets, dump the small functions fully, then run a whole-text call scan and read the enclosing function of each call site before naming. Keep the names file valid after every group of twenty-five.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Two shared stubs used everywhere as allocate and free carry unrelated native names in the database, and several helpers decode as garbage because they sit in the encrypted region; both had to be identified by usage shape rather than by name.

Verified The inventory overruns one function's size into padding and overlaps two jump-alias entries with their targets, and misses one self-recursive call, so entry sizes and callee counts needed independent checks.
